b: Renegade Game Studios is launching one of its biggest-ever retail marketing campaigns to capitalise on the success of its $13.3m Dungeon Crawler Carl crowdfunding project – while apologising to backers who have been frustrated by fulfilment delays and games reaching stores before their own pledges.

The publisher’s Carlsgiving initiative, running from today until the end of the year, will see Renegade pay for online adverts encouraging fans to visit their local game stores, alongside giveaways, in-store demonstrations and other promotional activities aimed at bringing the campaign’s more than 55,000 backers into shops.
Renegade’s marketing lead Jordan Gaeta told BoardGameWire the initiative was among its largest retail marketing investments to date, and could become a model for future launches if successful.
“We wanted to give game stores a real launch moment, not just a street date,” he said.

The initiative follows the extraordinary success of Renegade’s Dungeon Crawler Carl crowdfund, which raised $13.3m across the RPG and Unstoppable board game in May – becoming the biggest campaign in BackerKit’s history.
Gaeta said demand from retailers had also been stronger than expected, with some stores already selling through their initial stock.
But he added that some distributors had underestimated demand for the games, despite warnings from the publisher that they were likely to be strong sellers.

Gaeta said, “We printed many thousands more copies than distributors ordered. Distributors tend to be cautious with large orders on new lines. We told them this one would be in high demand, but many initial orders still came in conservative.”
He added that a second printing of Unstoppable had already arrived, with several other products in the range also going back to print.

The comments follow reports from hobby retailers of strong initial sales and difficulties obtaining replacement inventory, with others complaining that their initial deliveries would not arrive in time for the Carlsgiving promotion.
Gaeta said the stores that had already sold out were retailers who backed the crowdfunding campaign, and had received the full quantities they had paid for.
“For other stores, product is flowing through distribution with reprints in progress to keep shelves stocked,” he told BoardGameWire.

The publisher’s efforts to build on Dungeon Crawler Carl’s crowdfunding success have nevertheless been complicated by the scale of fulfilling the campaign, and criticism from individual backers who have seen the games available in stores before receiving their own orders.

Gaeta told BoardGameWire that Renegade’s fulfilment partners had shipped roughly 90,000 packages worldwide in six weeks – compared with about 50,000 packages typically shipped by the company’s US webstore over an entire year.
He added that US fulfilment was 98% complete as of last week, with the company’s partners shipping up to 2,500 orders a day and aiming to finish the remaining shipments by today.

The US accounts for about 80% of the campaign’s backers, but some customers in Canada, Europe, the UK and Australia are facing longer waits, with Renegade expecting to complete outstanding international fulfilment by the end of December.
Renegade insisted the international delays were unrelated to the size of the campaign, instead blaming problems with transport and shipping.
“Global logistics are always challenging, but they’re exceptionally difficult right now,” Gaeta said.

“A huge increase in the cost of diesel has driven up shipping costs and reduced the number of trucks running in some markets. Combined with port congestion, it took weeks to book transport to our fulfillment centers.”

The company said the November 23 retail release date primarily applied to North America, with Canadian stores being asked to delay general retail sales until early December, and conventional retail releases in Europe, the UK and Australia following crowdfunding fulfilment.

The decision to allow retailers who backed the crowdfunding campaign to begin selling their stock before individual backers received their pledges has also drawn criticism, particularly following earlier assurances that backers would be among the first to receive the games.

Renegade told backers as recently as October 30 that it remained on track to complete fulfilment by November 23, although it subsequently acknowledged that international shipments would extend beyond that date.

The publisher defended its decision to fulfil retailer pledges alongside those of individual customers, arguing that stores which committed money to the campaign were also backers and should not be penalised for their participation.
“Many made a significant investment early, and shipping their orders alongside individual backers is standard practice in crowdfunding,” Gaeta said.
“What isn’t standard is a campaign of this size. Because fulfillment ran six to eight weeks, some backers saw the game in stores that backed the campaign before their own copy arrived.
“We understand why that was frustrating, and we’re sorry. It certainly wasn’t our intent to frustrate anyone. We were trying to be fair to all backers, and we obviously fell short with some.”
Gaeta also acknowledged criticism of Carlsgiving’s celebratory messaging while some customers were still waiting for their pledges.
“We hear it, and we’re sorry to anyone still waiting on their pledge,” he said. “We never want anyone to feel overlooked, and Carlsgiving was never meant to celebrate at their expense.”

Renegade said it had retained the November 23 US retail launch date to avoid disrupting retailers who had planned around the release, and customers who had chosen to purchase the games through their local stores.

The publisher expects to finish outstanding international fulfilment before the end of the year, apart from several hundred backers whose payment cards were declined or who have yet to complete their pledge management.
It said the vast majority of backers had already received their games, and that the lessons learned from handling the campaign would inform future crowdfunding projects.
“We’re not going to rest until every backer has their games in hand,” Gaeta said. “We’ve learned from this experience, and we’ll use those lessons to make the next project fulfillment smoother.”
